\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Benchmark scores drive model selection, resource allocation, and research priorities for large language models, yet training data contamination undermines the validity of these scores in ways that current evaluation cannot quantify \citep{hendrycks2021mmlu,chang2025benchmarking}. When models encounter test items during training, observed accuracy conflates genuine capability with memorization, and practitioners have no principled way to determine how much of a reported score reflects real understanding. The problem is compounded by the scale of modern training corpora: trillion-token web crawls make contamination pervasive and instance-level measurement infeasible \citep{oren2024proving}. Post-hoc calibration that quantifies contamination effects despite imperfect detection is therefore essential for trustworthy evaluation.

Two developments make this gap urgent. First, \citet{sun2025emperor} systematically evaluate twenty contamination mitigation strategies (rephrasing, option shuffling, dynamic benchmark regeneration, and others) and demonstrate that none restores clean performance after contamination has occurred. This result forecloses the ``prevent contamination'' approach for models already trained on unrestricted web data. Second, contamination-free benchmarks \citep{white2024livebench} offer a partial solution but sacrifice the comparability and institutional knowledge accumulated around established benchmarks. Dynamic regeneration of test items may also be contaminated within weeks as web crawlers index benchmark repositories \citep{dong_2024_cdd}. The field therefore needs post-hoc statistical tools that can separate genuine ability from contamination artifacts on existing benchmarks.

Detection methods such as Min-K\%++ \citep{zhang_2024_minkpp}, ConStat \citep{dekoninck2024constat}, and Kernel Divergence Signatures \citep{choi_2025_kds} can flag contaminated items but stop at detection. They do not quantify how much scores are inflated or produce adjusted scores with uncertainty estimates. Score adjustment methods like DCR \citep{xu2025dcr} provide point corrections without uncertainty quantification or a principled measurement framework. IRT-based evaluation frameworks \citep{polo_2024_tinybenchmarks,habba_2025_growing_pains} apply psychometric ability estimation to improve evaluation efficiency, but they treat all items as equally trustworthy and ignore contamination entirely \citep{lalor_2024_irt_nlp}. These two research threads have developed in isolation: detection papers end at binary flags, while IRT papers assume clean data. No existing method bridges detection signals and a measurement-theoretic calibration framework to produce decontaminated ability estimates with credible intervals.

This paper asks: does calibrating contaminated scores require accurate per-item detection, or can a principled measurement model separate ability from noise more generally? We develop ContamCal to answer this question. Stage~1 fuses multiple detection signals into continuous per-item exposure scores via training-free Reciprocal Rank Fusion \citep{cormack_2009_rrf}, avoiding the meta-circularity of learned aggregators that would require the very contamination labels we lack. Stage~2 embeds these exposure scores as covariates in a contamination-augmented IRT model (2PL+$\gamma$) that jointly estimates latent ability $\theta$ and a domain-level contamination effect $\gamma_k$. Our experiments yield a clear answer: IRT ability estimation itself provides the dominant calibration benefit. Vanilla 2PL without any contamination parameter reduces calibration error on ARC by 53\% (MAE from 0.034 to 0.016), matching the full 2PL+$\gamma$ model. The calibration comes from IRT's measurement structure, which separates stable capability from item-level noise regardless of contamination modeling. The $\gamma$ parameter serves a complementary diagnostic role: it reveals the direction and relative magnitude of contamination effects across cognitive domains. As model pools grow to the sizes our identifiability analysis requires, these domain-level estimates will support targeted evaluation policies.

Our contributions are as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{IRT calibration decomposition.} We demonstrate that IRT ability estimation provides calibration benefit independent of whether contamination is explicitly modeled through $\gamma$. This value decomposition clarifies that the primary benefit of psychometric modeling for contaminated benchmarks lies in separating stable ability from item-level noise, not in the contamination correction itself.
    \item \textbf{Multi-signal exposure detection via RRF.} We develop a training-free signal fusion pipeline that combines embedding similarity, token-level surprisal, and self-critique signals into continuous per-item exposure scores applicable to any benchmark without auxiliary data requirements.
    \item \textbf{Detection signal failure modes.} We document a directional reversal in Min-K\%++ at model scales below 1.5B parameters (Cohen's $d = -1.55$ to $-1.98$), where the signal is actively misleading rather than merely ineffective. This finding has immediate practical consequences for contamination detection at small scales.
    \item \textbf{Identifiability boundaries and domain-level diagnosis.} Simulation studies establish that reliable $\gamma$ recovery requires signal AUC $\geq 0.55$ and $J \geq 50$, a threshold well above current LLM evaluation practice ($J = 8$--$30$). At our empirical $J = 13$, per-domain $\gamma$ estimates reveal directional heterogeneity across MMLU cognitive domains, with one domain (Social Sciences, $\gamma = -0.57$) reaching significance and providing preliminary evidence that contamination effects vary by cognitive demand. These results validate the identifiability analysis and chart a path toward domain-specific evaluation with larger model pools.
\end{enumerate}

On the mitigation side, \citet{sun2025emperor} systematically evaluate twenty approaches (rephrasing, option shuffling, dynamic construction) and find that none reliably restores clean performance, motivating post-hoc correction. DCR \citep{xu2025dcr} estimates decontaminated scores via fuzzy inference but produces point estimates without uncertainty quantification or domain-level diagnosis. ContamCal consumes detection signals as inputs and feeds them into a calibration framework that estimates decontaminated ability with credible intervals.

-Recent work has produced diverse signals for identifying benchmark data in LLM training corpora. Min-K\% \citep{shi_2023_minkprob} and its successor Min-K\%++ \citep{zhang_2024_minkpp} perform membership inference via token-level surprisal statistics, with the latter achieving stronger separation through normalized probability comparisons. ConStat \citep{dekoninck2024constat} measures accuracy gaps between original and paraphrased items to isolate surface memorization from genuine understanding. CDD and TED \citep{dong_2024_cdd} distinguish generalization from memorization through completion-based probes that test whether models can reproduce exact benchmark content. KDS \citep{choi_2025_kds} quantifies leakage via kernel divergence between model outputs on seen and unseen distributions. TS-Guessing \citep{deng_2024_tsguessing} identifies contamination through systematic evaluation of completion accuracy across temporal splits, revealing that many high-scoring models exhibit suspicious temporal patterns. Concurrent with our work, \citet{tao2025detecting} propose an entropy collapse method targeting RL-trained models, exploiting policy collapse across reasoning paths rather than binary self-evaluation confidence. These methods flag contamination at the item or benchmark level but do not diagnose domain-level effects or produce adjusted scores. ContamCal consumes detection signals as inputs (Stage~1) and feeds them into a calibration framework (Stage~2) that estimates decontaminated ability.

+Item Response Theory has gained traction as a principled alternative to raw accuracy. \citet{lalor_2024_irt_nlp} provide a comprehensive IRT tutorial for NLP; TinyBenchmarks \citep{polo_2024_tinybenchmarks} uses IRT-informed item selection for efficient evaluation; Growing Pains \citep{habba_2025_growing_pains} validates IRT at scale on 400+ models and identifies low-respondent limitations; HiBayES \citep{luettgau_2025_hibayes} adds hierarchical Bayesian inference for credible intervals; ATLAS \citep{li_2024_atlas} applies IRT for adaptive testing. All treat items as equally trustworthy. ContamCal augments IRT with contamination covariates $\gamma_k$ within the item response function, drawing on the educational measurement tradition of item compromise modeling \citep{eckerly_2017_item_compromise,sinharay_2017_preknowledge}, DIF cancellation \citep{ercikan_2008_dif_cancellation}, and explanatory IRT \citep{deboeck_2004_explanatory_irt}, with three adaptations for LLM evaluation: continuous exposure scores, domain-level effects, and counterfactual inference (\S\ref{sec:formulation}).

-Item Response Theory (IRT) has gained traction as a principled alternative to raw accuracy for comparing LLMs. \citet{lalor_2024_irt_nlp} provide a comprehensive tutorial on IRT in NLP evaluation, covering model selection, parameter estimation, and ability scoring. TinyBenchmarks \citep{polo_2024_tinybenchmarks} exploits IRT-informed item selection to reduce evaluation cost while preserving ranking fidelity across diverse model families. Growing Pains \citep{habba_2025_growing_pains} validates IRT at scale on 400+ models with fixed parameter calibration and identifies practical limitations in low-respondent regimes where item parameters become poorly constrained. HiBayES \citep{luettgau_2025_hibayes} extends IRT with hierarchical Bayesian inference to produce credible intervals over ability estimates, enabling principled model comparison under uncertainty. ATLAS \citep{li_2024_atlas} applies IRT for adaptive testing and selects maximally informative items to reduce per-model evaluation cost. Across this body of work, all items are treated as equally trustworthy: none models contamination as a covariate within the item response function. ContamCal augments IRT with per-domain contamination parameters $\gamma_d$ that separate genuine ability from exposure-driven inflation.

-The psychometric literature has long studied item compromise, where test content is disclosed before administration. \citet{eckerly_2017_item_compromise} develops IRT models that incorporate compromise indicators to jointly estimate item parameters and preknowledge effects, showing that ignoring compromise biases all estimated parameters. \citet{sinharay_2017_preknowledge} proposes likelihood ratio and score tests for item preknowledge detection at the individual level, establishing statistical power requirements for reliable identification. DIF cancellation \citep{ercikan_2008_dif_cancellation} demonstrates that item-level bias can aggregate unpredictably across test domains, motivating domain-level rather than item-level analysis. Explanatory IRT \citep{deboeck_2004_explanatory_irt} provides the theoretical foundation for embedding external covariates directly within item response functions. ContamCal adapts this tradition with three modifications for LLM evaluation: continuous exposure scores replace binary leaked/not-leaked indicators, effects are estimated at domain granularity rather than per-item, and counterfactual inference (setting exposure to zero) replaces group comparison, since LLMs lack a clean ``control group'' (Section~\ref{sec:formulation}).

-Mitigation strategies attempt to neutralize contamination at test time. \citet{sun2025emperor} systematically evaluate twenty approaches (item rephrasing, option shuffling, dynamic construction, filtering) across ten LLMs and five benchmarks; none reliably eliminates score inflation. This failure motivates post-hoc statistical correction rather than prevention. DCR \citep{xu2025dcr} is the most closely related method: it estimates decontaminated scores by combining detection signals with fuzzy inference rules. However, DCR produces point estimates without uncertainty quantification, does not model domain-level heterogeneity in contamination effects, and lacks IRT grounding that would connect score adjustment to a latent ability scale. No public implementation is available, so we compare qualitatively in Section~\ref{sec:results}. ContamCal addresses all three limitations through Bayesian IRT with per-domain $\gamma_d$ parameters and posterior credible intervals that propagate signal noise into final uncertainty bounds.

-We use ``calibration'' in the psychometric sense throughout this paper: adjusting benchmark scores to approximate clean (uncontaminated) performance. This differs from probability calibration in machine learning \citep{guo_2017_calibration}, where the goal is aligning predicted confidences with empirical frequencies via temperature scaling or Platt scaling. ContamCal performs score-level adjustment for contamination bias, not recalibration of output probabilities. We adopt this terminology following the educational measurement convention where ``calibration'' refers to placing items and examinees on a common scale after accounting for known distortions. Readers familiar with the ML calibration literature should note that our reliability diagrams (\S\ref{sec:results}) compare calibrated scores against held-out clean accuracy, not predicted probabilities against observed outcomes.
